label: Origin-tolerance rival with varied individual restored, against actual-world Euclidean access
summary: Closes the interpretation gap of the structural surrogate ToleranceOriginRival.Control.Certificate. Added an origin interface (OriginToleranceIdentity): origins per world and individual, a closeness relation near; commitments NearIsTolerance (reflexive, symmetric), OriginDeterminesAccess (access iff every shared individual has near origins), OriginPlenitude (every near variation realised in an accessible world) and VariedOriginAt (one actual concrete individual with non-near origins at two successors). Bridge originToleranceNonEuclidean (zero-axiom): NearIsTolerance, OriginDeterminesAccess and VariedOriginAt entail the surrogate frame condition ToleranceNonEuclideanAt. Outcome on the surrogate: restoring the varied individual at all three offsets (Control.restored) satisfies the four commitments but the individual exists at every successor of actual, so NecessaryConcreteAt holds there: the surrogate countermodel is destroyed under the restored commitment. Outcome on Arrival A: a faithful countermodel survives on five worlds with two rigidly identified individuals (Control.faithful): a with offsets -1/0/+1 at aMinus/actual/plus, b with offsets 0/0/-1/+1 at actual/plus/bMinus/bPlus; access fails only aMinus-plus and bMinus-bPlus. All four origin commitments, ActualReflexive, presence-to-existence, inert emptiness and the possible contingent-free past (witness plus, times 0<1: b necessary at plus and present throughout, a contingent at plus and present only at 1) hold; EuclideanAt and NecessaryConcreteAt fail at actual (a absent from bMinus, b absent from aMinus). General reason: the arrival delivers an individual necessary relative to the witness world v; without Euclidean access nothing forces it into a successor of actual that v does not see, and origin tolerance permits such a successor (the far-origin world of another individual) to lack it. Why two individuals (prose argument, not Lean-checked): under OriginDeterminesAccess, if c is necessary at v and u is a successor of actual lacking c, then v does not see u, so some individual y existing at v and u has far origins there; y differs from c since c is absent from u. Correction after semantic challenge: any countermodel to Arrival A needs two individuals, already forced by the arrival's premises (necessary-at-v and contingent-at-v individuals differ); the origin argument adds that the c-lacking successor must be cut off by a second individual's far origin; on a one-individual carrier the arrival's premises are unsatisfiable, so it holds only vacuously. Control.restored covers one assignment; the general three-world case is prose. Strongest objection (challenge): with a deletion/recombination plenitude principle no individual is necessary at any world, so the arrival's premises become jointly unsatisfiable and the rival would survive only vacuously; untested.
blocker: The countermodel uses permitted, not required, absences (b from aMinus, a from bMinus); OPEN whether a cross-world persistence bridge (an individual necessary at a possible world exists at every possibility of actual) is warranted independently of Euclidean access, and whether the if-half of OriginDeterminesAccess is part of the account. Counterpart, vague and kind-relative tolerance readings and the possible-external-cause arrival were not tested.
